t: Legislation 1: Consumer Contracts, Copyright and Computer Misuse
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCSE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson L21: Legislation 1: Consumer Contracts, Copyright and Computer Misuse.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Give the full, exact title of each law and say what it protects. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

Digital technology lets us shop, create and communicate easily, but it also makes it easy to cheat customers, copy other people's work and break into computers. Three laws in this lesson deal with these problems. The Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 protect people who buy online, by phone or by mail order. They must be given clear information before paying, they get 14 days to change their mind about most goods, and they cannot be charged hidden extras.
Makes sense. Keep going.

The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects intellectual property, such as software, music and images, so that only the owner can decide how it is copied or used. The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes it a crime to access or change a computer system without permission. Together with data protection law, covered in the next lesson, these are the laws you need to name and apply.
Right. What else do we need to know?

When you buy online you cannot see or handle the product, so the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 give you extra rights. Before you pay, the trader must give their identity and contact details, a description of the product, the full price including delivery, and how to cancel. Digital content must come with information about which devices it works with. For goods, the cooling-off period lasts 14 days from the day after delivery, and you do not need a reason to cancel. The refund must arrive within 14 days of the goods coming back or proof of posting.
Got it. Keep going.

There are exceptions. You lose the right to cancel a download once it starts, as long as you agreed to that. Unsealed DVDs, games and software, and personalised items cannot be returned unless faulty. Pre-ticked boxes for extra payments are banned. Since 2025 the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 has added further protection, such as banning fake reviews.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Copyright protects original work automatically from the moment it is created. Under the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 a computer program is treated as a literary work, so its code cannot be copied without the owner's permission. When you 'buy' software you are really buying a licence: a legal agreement saying how many people or computers may use it and for what purpose. A school might buy a network licence for 30 machines or a site licence for the whole campus.
Okay. Keep going.

Software piracy means illegally copying, downloading, sharing or selling software. Licence infringement includes installing software on more computers than allowed, sharing a licence key, using a student licence for business or carrying on after a subscription ends. Free software is not automatically free of copyright: freeware is still owned, while open-source licences allow the code to be changed and shared on stated terms. Breaches can lead to unlimited fines and, in serious cases, prison.
Go on.

The Computer Misuse Act 1990 was passed because, before it, hacking was hard to prosecute. It has since been updated. Section 1 makes unauthorised access to computer material an offence, even if nothing is changed. Section 2 covers unauthorised access with intent to commit a further crime, such as fraud or blackmail. Section 3 covers unauthorised acts that impair a computer, for example modifying or deleting data, spreading a virus, locking users out by changing their passwords, or launching a denial-of-service attack.
Right. Keep going.

Later additions cover acts that risk serious damage, for example to hospitals or power supplies (section 3ZA), and making or supplying hacking tools (section 3A). A hacker is someone who breaks into a system or its data without permission. A virus is malware that copies itself and damages files. Spyware secretly records a user's activity and sends it to someone else. Penalties rise with seriousness, from fines up to long prison sentences.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013?

The Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013: protect people who buy online, by phone or by mail order by requiring clear information, giving a 14-day right to cancel and banning hidden extra charges.
Cooling-off period?
The 14 days in which a consumer can cancel a distance purchase without giving a reason and get a refund; for goods it starts the day after delivery.
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988?
Protects the intellectual property of creators, including software, music, images and text, so it cannot be copied, shared, sold or adapted without the owner's permission.
Intellectual property?
Original creative work, such as software, music, designs or writing, which belongs to the person or organisation that created it.
Software licence?
A legal agreement that states how a piece of software may be used, including how many users or computers may run it.
Software piracy?
Illegally copying, downloading, distributing or selling software without the copyright owner's permission.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Questions on these laws have appeared in most recent papers. In the 2025 paper, question 9 candidates had to give the full title of the consumer law, and the examiners noted that many could not name it precisely, so learn 'Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013'. Scenario questions ask you to match a situation to the law broken: name the Act and its year, then link it to the detail in the scenario. Copyright has come up in the 2022 paper, question 9 and the 2023 paper, question 10, where marks were given for naming the Act and describing a breach such as installing software without a licence. the 2019 paper, question 1 and the 2021 paper, question 10 also tested consumer law and computer misuse. For a 'describe' question, make one point and then add detail or an example for the second mark. Common mistakes are mixing up the Computer Misuse Act with data protection and writing 'copywrite'.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. How long is the cooling-off period for most goods bought online under the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013? Is it A, 7 days; B, 28 days; C, 14 days; D, 30 days?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is C: 14 days. Consumers can cancel within 14 days, counted from the day after the goods are delivered.
That's it for Legislation 1: Consumer Contracts, Copyright and Computer Misuse. Next, try the worksheet and the quiz for this lesson on the hub.
Thanks for listening. See you next time.
